claims.text: Systematically lowering stacking-fault energy through controlled elemental substitution in dual-phase HEAs will promote transformation-induced plasticity and deformation twinning.
Transformation-induced plasticity and deformation twinning enhance toughness retention under demanding conditions.
The baseline material is a near-equiatomic dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy.
The baseline alloy exhibits degrading toughness at high strain rate and low temperature.
Limited activation of transformation-induced plasticity causes the baseline alloy's toughness degradation.
Adding a controlled fraction of Mn can lower the stacking-fault energy of the baseline alloy.
High strain rate and low temperature activate deformation mechanisms such as twinning and phase transformation.
Stacking-fault energy governs the balance among dislocation slip, deformation-induced transformation, and twinning.
Lowering stacking-fault energy facilitates transformation-induced plasticity.
Lowering stacking-fault energy facilitates the formation of deformation twins.
Transformation-induced plasticity and deformation twins delay crack initiation and propagation.
Higher stacking-fault energy limits transformation-induced plasticity and twinning, resulting in toughness loss.
A modest substitution-induced reduction in stacking-fault energy will improve toughness retention relative to the unsubstituted baseline.
The modified alloys will exhibit higher impact energy or fracture toughness than the baseline.
The modified alloys will exhibit more deformation twinning or transformation activity than the baseline.
The proposed relationship should hold at high strain rate and low temperature when phase instability and deformation-induced transformations are significant.
Outside the stated high-strain-rate and low-temperature regime, other mechanisms may dominate toughness behavior.
Interphase decohesion or brittle-phase formation may counteract the toughness benefit expected from lowering stacking-fault energy.
